title: Eight Central Banks Holding a Price: the Pool That Collapsed in March 1968

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was spent was reserves, to hold a number. After a run sent the London price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960, the Pool was formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks, which "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep the price at $35.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The compromise was the promise itself: since 1958 "countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce", with the United States responsible for keeping that price fixed. A convertibility pledge is only as good as the metal behind it, and the Pool existed because the market had begun to test it.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The intervention was the fog: a price maintained by coordinated central bank selling looks, to anyone reading the quote, like a market price. The essay records the parallel machinery of swap lines with nine central banks providing "up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and notes that "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility" — a temporary fix that was "a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system".
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The arrangement bought seven years. "The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued", and in that time the dollar's convertibility was treated as sound because its price did not move.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The ending was a two-tier fiction rather than an admission. Sterling devalued, a run on gold followed, France withdrew, and "The pool collapsed in March 1968." The seven remaining members then "agreed to formulate a two-tiered system", with central banks using gold only to settle international debts — one price for governments and another for everyone else. The gold window closed entirely in August 1971.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: Bretton Woods: fixed currencies against the dollar and the dollar fixed to gold at $35, with the United States carrying the convertibility obligation for the system.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The two-tier gold market of March 1968, and then the closing of the gold window in August 1971 — the end of the convertibility the Pool had been built to defend.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: Defending the price required selling reserves; selling reserves reduced the backing that made the price credible; the weaker the backing, the more the price had to be defended. The swap lines that were meant to bridge the gap grew into a standing facility, which the essay reads as the symptom rather than the cure.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That the gold price was secretly rigged by a cartel of central banks, and that the public was never told.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The price was indeed held by coordinated central bank intervention — but not secretly, and the source for that is a Federal Reserve publication stating it plainly: the London Gold Pool "was formed on November 1, 1961", consisted of eight named central banks, and "agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system" and keep gold at $35 an ounce. An arrangement whose membership, date, mechanism and purpose are published by one of its members is a policy, not a conspiracy. What the record does support is the thing the decoy gestures at without naming: the price people could observe was an administered price, it was administered until it could not be, and when it failed the response was a two-tier system that kept one price for central banks and let the other float.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: A run that sent the London gold price to $40 an ounce on 20 October 1960. The London Gold Pool formed on 1 November 1961 by eight central banks — Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France and the United States — pooling reserves to hold the price at $35. Parallel swap lines with nine central banks providing up to $900 million equivalent, which grew from a short-term facility into an intermediate-term one. Success for six years. Then sterling's devaluation, another run on gold, France's withdrawal, and the Pool's collapse in March 1968, followed by a two-tier system in which the seven remaining members used gold only to settle international debts. Convertibility ended altogether in August 1971.

citations.title: Federal Reserve History, "Nixon Ends Convertibility of U.S. Dollars to Gold and Announces Wage/Price Controls, August 1971", by Sandra Kollen Ghizoni
citations.quoteOrFact: Read from federalreservehistory.org. NOTE ON FIT: the essay's subject is August 1971, not March 1968. It is cited here because it contains the passage on the London Gold Pool, which is this node's subject, and nothing in this dossier is drawn from the essay beyond what it says about the Pool and the system around it. On the system: under Bretton Woods "countries agreed to keep their currencies fixed (but adjustable in exceptional situations) to the dollar, and the dollar was fixed to gold. Since 1958 ... countries settled their international balances in dollars, and U.S. dollars were convertible to gold at a fixed exchange rate of $35 an ounce." ON THE POOL ITSELF: "A run in the London gold market sent the price to $40 an ounce on October 20, 1960, exacerbating the threat to the system. In response, the London Gold Pool was formed on November 1, 1961. The pool consisted of a group of eight central banks (Great Britain, West Germany, Switzerland, the Netherlands, Belgium, Italy, France, and the United States). In order to keep the price of gold at $35 an ounce, the group agreed to pool gold reserves to intervene in the London gold market in order to maintain the Bretton Woods system. The pool was successful for six years until another gold crisis ensued. The British pound sterling devalued and another run on gold occurred, and France withdrew from the pool. The pool collapsed in March 1968. At that time the seven remaining members of the London Gold Pool ... agreed to formulate a two-tiered system." On the swap lines that ran alongside it: credit lines with nine central banks "provided up to $900 million equivalent in foreign exchange", and "What started as a small, short-term credit facility grew to be a large, intermediate-term facility until the U.S. gold window closed in August 1971. The growth and need for the swap lines signaled that they were not just a temporary fix, but a sign of a fundamental problem in the monetary system." SOURCE CHARACTER: Federal Reserve History is an educational project of the Federal Reserve System. This is a signed secondary essay with its own bibliography, not a primary record, and it is tiered and attributed accordingly: the dossier says what the essay states, not what a contemporaneous document shows.
